title: Modify Authentication Process: Reversible Encryption
summary: Active Directory normally stores account passwords as the output of a one-way function, so the stored value cannot be turned back into the original password. The AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption account property changes that behaviour and keeps a recoverable copy of the password, a feature that exists only for legacy protocols needing the original secret. When the property is enabled and the user then sets or changes the password, the directory keeps an encrypted value in the account parameters along with a randomly generated component, while the remaining key material sits in a domain-wide secret and a static value inside a system library. An adversary who can read those elements together can reconstruct the key and recover the password. Attackers enable the property through group policy, a fine-grained password policy, or a directory command, then wait for the next password change. The change shows up in directory object changes and in policy or directory service logs, and it violates a well understood baseline, because the setting is off by default and rarely needed. Alerting on any account where it turns on is the strongest detection.

beginner.definition: Normally a Windows domain stores passwords in a form that cannot be turned back into the real password. This setting changes that behaviour and keeps a version that can be reversed. This technique means an attacker turns the setting on and later recovers real passwords.
beginner.whyItMatters: Once the setting is on, passwords for those accounts can be read in their original form. The recovered passwords often belong to administrators or to service accounts that are hard to change. The setting is easy to switch on and can go unnoticed for months. It also reduces the value of every other password protection measure you have put in place.
howItWorks: Windows domains normally keep only a one-way value that cannot be reversed into the password.
One account setting asks the domain to keep a recoverable copy of the password instead.
The copy is stored with a random element attached to the user account data.
The rest of the key material lives in a domain secret and a fixed value in a library.
An attacker enables the setting for chosen accounts through policy or a directory command.
After the next password change, they gather the parts and work out the real password.
beginner.example: Imagine a workplace that normally shreds each visitor form after recording a reference number. That reference number is enough to confirm a visitor later, and the original details are gone. A manager decides instead to keep a copy of every form in a locked cabinet. The forms are still filed properly and the cabinet door is locked. But now anybody who reaches the cabinet can read every form inside it. So can anybody who collects all of its keys.
takeaways: Reversible password encryption should stay disabled unless a documented legacy need exists.
Alert whenever this property becomes enabled for any account.
Recovered passwords live outside the directory, so rotate affected accounts immediately.

objectives: Explain the difference between one-way hashing and reversible encryption of passwords.
Describe where the recoverable password material is stored in a Windows domain.
Recognise the ways the setting can be enabled, including policy and directory commands.
Identify the directory and policy records that reveal the change.
Justify keeping the setting disabled as a baseline control.
